sbh3.1:0.2: The Nine Stages of Mental Abiding
sbh3.1:1.1: One-pointedness [citta-ekāgratā] has both the side of śamatha (calm-abiding) and the side of vipaśyanā (insight).
sbh3.1:1.2: The one-pointedness of the nine-fold mental abiding [navākārā citta-sthiti] belongs to the śamatha side; the one-pointedness of the four-fold support of wisdom belongs to the vipaśyanā side.
sbh3.1:2.1: What is the nine-fold mental abiding?
sbh3.1:2.2: Here a monk places [sthāpayati] the mind inwardly,
sbh3.1:2.4: places it again [avasthāpayati], places it closely [upasthāpayati],
sbh3.1:3.2: Withdrawing it from all external objects, he ties it inwardly toward non-distraction.
sbh3.1:3.3: That first binding [of the mind] against distraction — this is placement.
sbh3.1:4.1: How does he place it continuously?
sbh3.1:4.2: That mind first bound is strong, gross, unsettled, and not fully settled. On that very same object, through the practice of strengthening and the practice of clarification, with deliberate restraint — making it subtle and gathering it together — he places it continuously.
sbh3.1:5.1: How does he place it again?
sbh3.1:5.2: If, while he is placing the mind,
sbh3.1:5.3: it becomes distracted outwardly through loss of mindfulness.
sbh3.1:6.2: By those signs which distract his mind —
sbh3.1:6.3: namely the signs of wandering objects of contact, and the signs of passion, hatred, delusion, and of women and men —
sbh3.1:6.4: having previously grasped the perception of their danger,
sbh3.1:6.5: and taking that as governing, he does not allow the mind to spread out toward those signs.
sbh3.1:7.2: By those thoughts — sensual thoughts and the like —
sbh3.1:7.4: sensual desire, the hindrances, and so forth —
sbh3.1:7.5: there is agitation of the mind.
sbh3.1:7.6: Having previously grasped the perception of their danger,
sbh3.1:7.9: he does not allow [the mind] to spread out — thus he pacifies it.
sbh3.1:8.2: When through loss of mindfulness both [thoughts and defilements] occur and arise, he does not tolerate them as they arise;
sbh3.1:9.1: How does he make [the mind] single-pointed?
sbh3.1:9.2: With deliberate effort, he establishes a continuous, unbroken, uninterrupted flow of samādhi — thus he makes it single-pointed.
sbh3.1:10.2: Through following on cultivation, through following on practice, through following on repeated application — [he attains] effortless flow,
sbh3.1:10.3: flow carried by its own essence;
sbh3.1:10.5: by which, without deliberate effort, without exertion, the flow of his mind's samādhi
sbh3.1:11.1: The nine-fold mental abiding is accomplished through the six kinds of power [ṣaḍ-vidha-bala] —
sbh3.1:11.2: namely the power of hearing [śruta-bala] and the power of thinking [cintā-bala], the power of mindfulness [smṛti-bala] [and the power of clear comprehension (samprajanya-bala)], the power of diligence [vīrya-bala], and the power of familiarity [paricaya-bala].
sbh3.1:12.1: Through the power of hearing-and-thinking, then:
sbh3.1:12.2: taking what he has heard and what he has reflected on as governing, from the very beginning he places the mind on the object;
sbh3.1:12.4: by sustained engagement, he places it continuously.
sbh3.1:12.5: When the bound mind drifts, through the power of mindfulness he draws it back, placing it again
sbh3.1:12.7: Then through the power of clear comprehension [samprajanya-bala], not allowing the mind to spread toward distracting signs, thoughts, and defilements, he tames
sbh3.1:12.10: not tolerating their occurrence at all, he fully pacifies
sbh3.1:12.12: Through the power of familiarity, he concentrates.
sbh3.1:13.1: In the nine-fold mental abiding, four modes of mental engagement should be known:
sbh3.1:13.2: forcible engagement, interrupted engagement, uninterrupted engagement, and effortless engagement.
sbh3.1:14.1: In one who is placing and placing continuously, the mode of engagement is forcible (bala-vāhana).
sbh3.1:14.2: In one who is placing again, placing closely, taming, pacifying, or fully pacifying, the mode of engagement is interrupted (sacchidra-vāhana).
sbh3.1:14.3: In one who is making single-pointed, the mode of engagement is uninterrupted (niścchidra-vāhana).
sbh3.1:14.4: In one who is concentrating, the mode of engagement is effortless (anābhoga-vāhana).
sbh3.1:15.1: Thus these [four modes] in mental abiding belong to the śamatha side.
sbh3.1:15.2: But for one who, having attained inward calm-abiding, then applies himself to vipaśyanā —
sbh3.1:15.3: for him these very same four modes belong to the vipaśyanā side.
